newsitem.title: USA: Venezuelan bank fraud case nears close.
newsitem.headline: Venezuelan bank fraud case nears close.

text.p: Prosecutors on Thursday delivered closing arguments in a bank fraud case against a Cuban-born banker, his son and grandson, bringing the lengthy and complex financial case near its conclusion.
The jury was expected to begin deliberating the charges against Orlando Castro Llanes, Orlando Castro Castro and Castro Barredo on Friday.

They are accused of illegally using deposits in a family-controlled bank, Banco Progreso International de Puerto Rico (BPIPR) to prop up financial institutions they controlled in Central and South America.
Manhattan Supreme Court Judge Edward McLaughlin told the jurors he would give them instructions on Friday morning. The panel has heard 44 witnesses during four months of testimony.
Prosecutors say the three misled Venezuelan depositors to believe BPIPR was a safe off-shore bank, subject to tight regulatory control, and attracted deposits of more than $55 million.
The Puerto Rican bank closed down in January 1995 with uninsured loses to depositors of more than $15 million.
"It was a massive fraud," prosecutor Richard Preiss said. "These three fiddlers sitting at the defence table tried to shift the blame for the scheme by blaming everyone."
He accused them of playing a financial "musical chair game" to prop up their banking empire.
Defence attorneys claim the charges are revenge by the Venezuelan government.
Richard Sharpstein, lawyer for the eldest Castro, danced the Macarena as he ridiculed the prosecution's case and blamed liquidators for the bank's demise.
"It's not us who is running these people around seeking their money. It's the liquidators who have all the money. They just won't give it back," he said.

A key issue facing jurors is whether New York has jurisdiction in the case. Manhattan District Attorney Robert Morgenthau has argued that millions of dollars in the alleged frauds were transferred through New York banks.
The defence claims no one in New York was defrauded.
Morgenthau has said he took on the case at the request of the Venezuelan government.
"When a national government has lost $7 billion and the attorney general says to you, 'Will you help us?' you've got to respond yes if you have jurisdiction and I think we did," Morgenthau said.

Castro, a Cuban exile accused of playing a key role in Venezuela's 1994 banking crisis, left Venezuela that year after arrest warrants were issued for him and several associates on charges of financial fraud and other crimes.
All three have been in jail since their arrests in April.
